Last month I tried an experiment where I left my laptop at my desk and walked in with a single index card for notes. Within a week the rest of the team started closing their screens too, everyone actually paid attention, and our meetings got noticeably shorter. evals.prompt: Write an Instagram Reels voiceover script about junior developers relying on AI coding tools to write every line for them. Check what people are currently saying about this lately to sharpen the hook and angle. Story: I mentored a bright junior developer who started shipping features fast as soon as they turned on AI autocomplete, and at first our whole team celebrated their velocity. Then a production bug hit a 40-line function they had pushed that morning. When they tried to debug it, they pasted the error back into AI three times, made the bug worse, and admitted they couldn't explain what half of their own function did. Core message: shipping fast means nothing if you skip building the mental model to debug what you put in production. Takeaway: write the core logic of a tricky feature yourself before using AI to clean it up.

evals.prompt: Write a YouTube Shorts voiceover script from this story: Early in running my freelance video studio, I billed every client by the hour because it felt fair and transparent. The faster and sharper I got at editing, the less money I made on every project. One quarter I invested weeks learning faster workflows, delivered a launch cut to a repeat client in half the usual time, and sent an invoice that was half my normal pay even though their campaign performed better than anything I had made for them before. Meanwhile, slower freelancers were billing double for weaker work. That invoice broke hourly billing for me. On my very next proposal, I quoted a flat project fee tied to the deliverables and turnaround instead of my timesheet, and the client approved it the same afternoon without questioning my hours. Core message: hourly billing punishes you for getting good at your craft and aligns clients around watching the clock instead of valuing the result. Takeaway: on your next client proposal, replace your hourly rate with one flat price tied to clear deliverables.
